source_read: PMC HTML (PMC6148333), full text read in my own browser tab: Summary, Introduction, Research in context panel, Methods, Results (three subsections), Discussion, Conclusion, funding, acknowledgments, contributors and declaration of interests; figures 1-5 known from their legends only (no values read from them); appendices 1-2 not read. The PMC page carries notices of two corrections (Lancet 2018;392:1116 and 2019;393:e44), which were not read.

claims.note: Only the closing GBD 2016 sentence rests on this source. Both shares and intervals match. They are shares of alcohol-attributable deaths at ages 50 and older (not of all cancer deaths), modelled against a minimum-risk level of zero drinks; the claim words them correctly ('of the deaths attributed to alcohol') and labels them as a model in the magnitude.

anchors.locator: Results > Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: At ages 50 and older, cancers made up 27.1% (95% UI 21.2-33.3) of alcohol-attributable deaths in females and 18.9% (15.3-22.6) in males in 2016; cancers were the main source of attributable burden in high-SDI countries, tuberculosis then cirrhosis in low-SDI countries.

anchors.locator: Summary > Findings
anchors.extracted: Same two figures for ages 50 and older: 27.1% (21.2-33.3) of female and 18.9% (15.3-22.6) of male alcohol-attributable deaths were cancers.

claims.overstatement: 'fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer' should say 'every cancer it included': GBD 2016 modelled only outcomes it judged causal by Bradford Hill criteria (23 outcomes, listed in appendix 1), so cancers for which pooled studies show lower figures at light drinking (kidney, thyroid, lymphomas) were not among its curves. The main text says nothing about statistical significance at low intake for the cancer curves.
claims.note: That the GBD review drew on 'an overlapping set of studies' cannot be checked in the main text: the included studies are listed only in appendix 1 (not read); the paper says it searched PubMed, the GHDx and the references of previously published meta-analyses, which makes overlap likely but does not show it.

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Apart from the J-shaped curves for ischaemic heart disease (significant) and diabetes and ischaemic stroke (non-significant), relative risk rose monotonically with consumption for all other outcomes, all cancers included; per-outcome curves only in appendix 2.

anchors.locator: Methods > Study design, 2nd paragraph; Methods > Data sources, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Outcomes chosen by reviewing studies and applying Bradford Hill criteria; 23 outcomes, listed with sources in appendix 1. Search for the meta-analysis: PubMed, GHDx and references of previous meta-analyses; 3992 relative-risk estimates from 592 studies (28 million people, 649 000 cases).

claims.note: The GBD sentence is accurate as worded ('every cancer it included'). 'Whose own review of studies overlaps with this one' cannot be verified from the main text (study list in appendix 1, not read; search included references of earlier meta-analyses).

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: For every outcome other than ischaemic heart disease, diabetes and ischaemic stroke, all cancers included, relative risk increased monotonically with consumption.

anchors.locator: Methods > Study design, 2nd paragraph; Methods > Data sources, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 23 outcomes selected with Bradford Hill criteria (list in appendix 1); 592 studies found through PubMed, the GHDx and references of earlier meta-analyses.

claims.note: Every GBD 2016 number in the statement and magnitude matches (2.8 million, 2.4-3.3; 2.2%, 1.5-3.0; 6.8%, 5.8-8.0; DALYs 1.6%, 1.4-2.0 and 6.0%, 5.4-6.7; ages 15-49 deaths 3.8%, 3.2-4.3 and 12.2%, 10.8-13.6; tuberculosis 1.4%, 1.0-1.7, road injuries 1.2%, 0.7-1.9, self-harm 1.1%, 0.6-1.5; TMREL 0, 0.0-0.8 drinks of 10 g a day). Recomputed: 2.2% is about 2 in 100 and 6.8% about 7 in 100, as stated. Rank: seventh for both deaths and DALYs (Summary), first at ages 15-49 (by attributable burden). The paper's intervals come from 1000 draws carrying sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation; the claim's statement that the paper does not say they include model-structure or study-bias uncertainty is correct, but for balance it could add that hyper-parameter and parameter uncertainty are included. The underestimate list in the claim is a subset: the authors also name unrecorded consumption, US-only data for harm to others on the roads, and outcomes left out such as dementia and psoriasis. Not from this source: 'more than a quarter of the world's drinking' unrecorded and 'mostly of middle-class cohorts in high-income countries' (presumably Rehm 2009). Funding: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation; acknowledgments add an NIA grant (P30AG047845).

anchors.locator: Results > Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: 2016: 2.8 million deaths (95% UI 2.4-3.3) attributed to alcohol; 2.2% (1.5-3.0) of age-standardised female and 6.8% (5.8-8.0) of male deaths; 1.6% (1.4-2.0) and 6.0% (5.4-6.7) of DALYs; seventh-ranked risk factor; at ages 15-49 the leading risk factor, 8.9% (7.8-9.9) of male and 2.3% (2.0-2.6) of female DALYs, 3.8% (3.2-4.3) of female and 12.2% (10.8-13.6) of male deaths.

anchors.locator: Summary > Findings
anchors.extracted: Seventh leading risk factor for both deaths and DALYs in 2016; leading risk factor at ages 15-49; leading attributable causes of death at 15-49: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0-1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7-1.9), self-harm 1.1% (0.6-1.5) of total deaths; TMREL zero (0.0-0.8), printed here as per week rather than per day.

anchors.locator: Results > Global patterns in alcohol-attributable deaths and disease burden, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: The three leading causes of attributable deaths in the age group under discussion: tuberculosis 1.4% (1.0-1.7), road injuries 1.2% (0.7-1.9), self-harm 1.1% (0.6-1.5) of total deaths; the age group is identified as 15-49 only in the Summary.

anchors.locator: Methods > Data sources, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Methods > Attributable burden due to alcohol use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Exposure modelled from sales-based alcohol stock (adjusted for tourists and for unrecorded consumption, sampled from 0 to the average of published estimates) rescaled with survey prevalence and amounts; PAFs computed from exposure, relative-risk curves and the TMREL, then multiplied by cause-specific deaths and DALYs; alcohol use disorders assigned a PAF of 1.

anchors.locator: Methods > Uncertainty analysis
anchors.extracted: Uncertainty from 1000 draws reflecting sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation; intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Nothing on uncertainty from model structure or bias in the underlying studies.

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph; Methods > Systematic review and meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: TMREL defined as the minimum of a weighted all-outcome relative-risk curve (weights: global age-standardised 2016 DALY rates, both sexes); estimated at zero (95% UI 0.0-0.8) standard drinks of 10 g a day.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Limitations: unrecorded consumption incompletely captured; drinking patterns assumed constant; road harm to others based on US data only; no data on harm to others from interpersonal violence; under-15s not assessed; outcomes such as dementia and psoriasis not included; together likely to make results underestimates.

claims.note: The GBD figures match (0.86, 0.80-0.96 at 0.83 drinks a day in men; 0.82, 0.72-0.95 at 0.92 in women; only ischaemic heart disease significant of 23 outcomes). Reference group: the statement does not name it for the GBD sentence; the magnitude does ('each study's non-drinking category, adjusted for former drinkers in it'), which matches the source's study-level covariate for whether the reference category included former drinkers, retained for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes. Indirectness: the 592 GBD studies are 'prospective and retrospective', so the GBD curve is not confined to the prospective cohorts named in the claim's population.

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only ischaemic heart disease had a statistically significant J-shaped curve: minimum relative risk 0.86 (0.80-0.96) in men at 0.83 and 0.82 (0.72-0.95) in women at 0.92 standard drinks a day; diabetes and ischaemic stroke non-significant J shapes; no difference in the IHD or diabetes curves by age.

anchors.locator: Methods > Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph; Summary > Methods
anchors.extracted: Mixed-effects logistic regression with splines from 0 to 12.5 drinks a day; a study-level covariate for reference-category composition (for example former drinkers counted as abstainers) kept where significant: IHD, ischaemic stroke, diabetes. Sources: 592 prospective and retrospective studies.

claims.note: The source confirms that GBD 2016 assumed constant drinking patterns within a year and did not model heavy drinking occasions.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Second limitation: drinking patterns within a year assumed consistent, although patterns rather than average amounts may carry different risks; data on patterns by age, sex and location, and prospective studies measuring pattern and average together, are lacking.

claims.note: The statement does not cite this source; it serves only as a qualifier showing the dispute and the reference-group problem. Caution if it is ever used as evidence on deaths from all causes: the Interpretation says all-cause mortality risk rises with consumption, but the paper presents no all-cause mortality analysis; its weighted curve combines 23 outcome curves weighted by DALY rates.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Earlier all-cause studies and meta-analyses suggesting protection at low or moderate intake are described as limited by small samples, inadequate confounder control and non-optimal reference categories; more recent work (Mendelian randomisation, pooled cohorts, multivariable-adjusted meta-analyses) increasingly shows non-significant or no protective effect on all-cause mortality or cardiovascular outcomes.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Summary > Interpretation
anchors.extracted: Most earlier meta-analyses did not control for the composition of the reference category (sick quitter hypothesis, survival bias); GBD 2016 added covariates for reference category and mean age. The Interpretation states that all-cause mortality risk rises with consumption, without a separate all-cause analysis in the paper.

claims.note: All GBD 2016 numbers match (23 outcomes, 592 studies, 3992 relative-risk estimates; TMREL 0, 0.0-0.8 drinks a day, printed per week in the Summary; IHD minima 0.86 and 0.82 at 0.83 and 0.92 drinks; non-significant dips for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; all cancers rising; weights global age-standardised 2016 DALY rates, both sexes). Offset in women: the Results name cancers; the Discussion adds injuries and communicable disease, so the claim's 'mainly by cancers' is acceptable. The claim's reading (not one person's risk) fits the method but not the authors' own framing: they describe the TMREL as the amount that minimises an individual's total attributable risk and conclude that 'the safest level of drinking is none'; the claim could say that the authors present it as individual risk. Supporting the claim's weights reading: in a sensitivity analysis the weighted curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Weighted curve minimised at zero (95% UI 0.0-0.8) standard drinks a day and rising monotonically; protective IHD and diabetes effects in females offset by monotonically rising cancer risks; sensitivity analysis: curve changed significantly only where diabetes and IHD exceeded 60% of total deaths.

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only IHD significantly J-shaped (minimum RR 0.86, 0.80-0.96, men, at 0.83 drinks; 0.82, 0.72-0.95, women, at 0.92); diabetes and ischaemic stroke non-significant J shapes; all other outcomes including all cancers monotonically rising.

anchors.locator: Methods > Systematic review and meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph; Methods > Data sources, 1st paragraph; Summary > Findings
anchors.extracted: TMREL = minimum of one weighted all-outcome curve, weights from global age-standardised DALY rates per 100 000 in 2016, both sexes; 3992 relative-risk estimates from 592 studies; the Summary prints the TMREL as zero (0.0-0.8) drinks per week, the Results per day.

anchors.locator: Introduction, 7th paragraph; Conclusion
anchors.extracted: Authors present the TMREL as the amount that minimises a person's total attributable risk of health loss (not a population average), and conclude that not drinking at all is safest.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Drinking patterns not modelled (constant within a year); dementia and psoriasis among outcomes not included; results likely underestimates.

claims.note: Matches: ischaemic stroke had a non-significant J-shaped curve in GBD 2016. No values for stroke are given in the main text.

anchors.locator: Results > Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Non-significant J-shaped curves for diabetes and ischaemic stroke; only IHD significant; values in appendix 2 only.

key_findings.correction: Numbers match Methods > Data sources, 1st paragraph and Study design, 2nd paragraph; 'prospective and retrospective' is worded so in Summary > Methods, and 195 locations, 1990-2016, ages 15 to 95 and older in Summary > Background and Introduction, 7th paragraph.

Drop 'net': the source describes protective effects for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes themselves (negative attributable burden for those causes in Figure 3), in females beyond age 60, particularly in high-SDI locations, not a net effect across causes; for males, the ischaemic heart disease effect in high- and low-SDI locations is called small compared with the total attributable burden there.
Minor: the Results say the protective effects were offset by cancer risks (no 'mainly'); the Discussion, 2nd paragraph, names cancer, injuries and communicable disease.

Checked the two notices on PMC (PMC6902241: Alan D Lopez added, names of Masood Ali Shaikh and Dhirendra Narain Sinha corrected, one affiliation updated, raw data on Mendeley Data, data-sharing statement added, online version corrected 27 September 2018; PMC6598857: Stefan Lorkowski added with affiliation and declaration, 20 June 2019). Neither notice changes a number. The PMC text is the uncorrected original (no Lopez or Lorkowski, uncorrected spellings, no data-sharing statement). The number-by-number comparison with the corrected online version was not repeated by this reader.

reporting_issues.note: Summary > Findings per week, Results > Health risks, 2nd paragraph, per day; 0.8 a day = 5.6 a week, recomputed. That the corrected online version still prints both was not checked by this reader.

Conclusion: nearly 10% of deaths at 15-49; Results give 3.8% (female) and 12.2% (male) only. Editors' arithmetic: a both-sexes share would lie between 3.8% and 12.2% and would reach 10% only if men made up about 74% of deaths at these ages ((10-3.8)/(12.2-3.8)); the paper gives no death counts by sex to check this.
The Discussion, 1st paragraph, uses a third wording (nearly 9% of all attributable DALYs for men, more than 2% for women).

The same wording is also in the Results, so the inconsistency is not only Discussion against Results: Results > Global patterns, 2nd paragraph (females experienced some protective effects for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes beyond 60) and Results > Health risks, 2nd paragraph (the weighted curve took into account protective effects for both in females) describe diabetes as protective, while Results > Health risks, 1st paragraph, calls its J shape non-significant. Sex-specific significance of the diabetes curve is not stated; consequence (minor overstatement for diabetes) unchanged.

Verified: data sources appendix 1 pp 52-140 (Study design, 2nd; Data sources, 1st) against curves appendix 2 pp 52-140 (Health risks, 1st); search and curves appendix 1 pp 57-146 (Systematic review, 1st) against appendix 2 pp 57-146 (Health risks, 1st; Figure 4 legend); SDI quintiles appendix 1 pp 8-12 (Attributable burden, 1st) against appendix 2 pp 8-12 (Results, consumption trends, 2nd).
PMC text: no Alan D Lopez or Stefan Lorkowski among collaborators; prints 'Masood A Ali Shaikh' and 'Dhirendra Narain Narain Sinha', the two names the 2018 notice corrected; no data-sharing section.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agrees with my reading: the headline minimum rests on observational relative-risk curves adjusted for reference-group composition in only three outcomes, and on one unvalidated global weighting whose own sensitivity check (curve shifts where IHD and diabetes exceed 60% of deaths) and the 2022 update (0.534 drinks a day with the 2016 curves) show it is weight-dependent. Domain judgments agree; 'sensitivity of the headline result' could be argued as some concerns, since the authors did report one sensitivity analysis, but the overall rating does not depend on it.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One gap to add: the Summary > Interpretation states that the risk of all-cause mortality rises with consumption, but the paper presents no all-cause mortality analysis; its weighted curve combines 23 outcome curves weighted by DALY rates (the card notes elsewhere, under outcomes, that all-cause mortality was not analysed).

missed: Summary > Interpretation: says the study found that all-cause mortality risk rises with consumption; no all-cause mortality analysis is reported (the weighted curve is DALY-weighted across 23 outcomes). Belongs in the interpretation gap and matters for any claim on deaths from all causes.

Introduction, 6th paragraph and Research in context: the authors present the estimated counterfactual as giving tangible evidence for low-risk drinking recommendations, yet report its minimum as zero; worth noting beside the individual-risk framing already in the interpretation gap.
